subsubtopic: BRITISH COLUMBIA LAND CLAIMS TRIAL-FUNDING SHORTAGE EXPERIENCED BY PLAINTIFFS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Gitksan-Wet'suwet'en Indian bands are seeking through court action recognition of their rights to their traditional lands in northern British Columbia.
The Government of Canada, as the trustee for Indian people under our Constitution, has an obligation to see that justice is done and that this case is heard in its entirety. The defendants in this case are both the province and the federal Government.
Three weeks into the trial the Department of Indian and Northern Affairs reduced its legal aid support to the bands by more than $1 million. The presiding judge, Chief Justice Allan McEachern of the B.C. Supreme Court, says it is imperative and in the public interest that this trial continue. He went on to say that anything other than that is a confession of failure on the part of all of us, and all those who support the justice system in our country.
Both the plaintiffs, that is the Indian bands, and the public must have a resolution of this vital question related to aboriginal rights. Therefore I ask that the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. McKnight) not try to win this case by reducing the funding for legal costs required by the Indian bands.

subsubtopic: CALL FOR EARLY PASSAGE OF LEGISLATION
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on June 29 I rose in this House to make the record clear about the Government's commendable action on war criminal legislation.
Unlike previous Governments we had the moral courage to set up a special commission chaired by Mr. Justice Jules Des-chenes to investigate the delicate issue of the possibility of war criminals living in Canada and to make recommendations concerning the prosecution of such individuals.
Our current Minister of Justice (Mr. Hnatyshyn) responded to the recommendations in a sensitive manner while insisting on a made-in-Canada solution. Bill C-71 provides the required legislation. Unfortunately, we were not able to pass this legislation in the last days of June due to some genuine concerns by two of my colleagues.
Since Parliament has been recalled to deal with the refugee legislation, I urge the Government and both opposition Parties to support quick passage of Bill C-71 during this emergency sitting. I spoke to the Minister of Justice this morning and he assured me that Bill C-71 is ready to be presented to the House of Commons. Let us get on with this historically important task.

subsubtopic: ELIGIBILITY FOR IRRIGATION PAYMENTS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Government's recent decision to provide supplementary benefits to irrigated production under the Special Canadian Grains Program appeared to be a good decision. Perhaps it was a good decision, but on the surface it now appears to be flawed. In what appears to be a hallmark of the Government, it has again clouded the issue.
For some unknown reason 80 per cent of Saskatchewan's intensively irrigated acreage is not eligible for supplementary benefits under the Special Canadian Grains Program. Irrigation farmers in Saskatchewan want to know why they are not eligible for these special payments. In Alberta only 20 per cent of intensely irrigated acreage is not eligible for these special benefits.
Why is there a discrepancy between Alberta and Saskatchewan under this program? If there is a good reason, why has the Government not bothered to tell the producers?

August 19, 1987

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
subsubtopic: OPPOSITION TO TAX ON FOOD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the White Paper on Tax Reform tabled on June 18 this year, the Conservative Government promised to reduce our taxes by $5 billion. It forgot to mention that since 1984, the Government has taken $22 billion from Canadian taxpayers.
Once again, the present Government is trying to throw up a smoke screen by pretending to reduce expenditures, although it is actually increasing the amount of money Canadians must spend by $17 billion.
As if that were not enough, the proposed reform includes a new federal sales tax, to be applied to goods and services. Despite representations made by the Opposition, the Government has refused to promise not to tax food. When we know that 46.8 per cent or nearly half of our senior citizens live below the poverty line, and that more than 16 per cent of their expenditures are for food, taxing this vital element of our daily lives would further aggravate the financial burden of these Canadians who spent their lives building our country. This tax is unacceptable and it is unfair. While the Government is reducing corporate taxes, it is increasing taxes for single
parent families and low-income families, in fact, it is taking the bread out of the mouths of those Canadians who are in greatest need.

subsubtopic: CONDEMNATION OF PRACTICES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Freshwater Fish Marketing Corporation ill serves fishermen in the Northwest Territories.
It has a stranglehold over their lives and seems almost useless at its stated purpose of marketing fish.
Its monopoly, granted by previous Governments, stamps out any private marketing initiative which would lead to higher prices being paid to fishermen.
The recent decision not to open the Wool Bay receiving station on Great Slave Lake goes against any economic sense and constitutes a threat to the livelihood of fishermen. The only reason can be that the corporation is deliberately trying to cut back production because of its failure to fulfil its sales mandate.
It is time that we removed this millstone from around the necks of northern fishermen.

subsubtopic: INSTITUTION OF MINIMUM INCOME PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, all Canadian men and women must be rejoicing at the Canadian Council on Social Development's recent report featuring recommendations pertaining to work and income. Canadian Council officials stress that four million Canadians live below the poverty level and they advocate the establishment of a minimum income program providing basic support payments for people who are unable to work, cannot find employment, or hold unpaid jobs like those who have to remain at home.
The income security system endorsed by the Canadian Council would make a significant contribution to families with children as well as to low- and middle-income households, and it would mark the end of the scandalous situation of poor children in this country.
Mr. Speaker, I am delighted that business circles and labour leaders have welcomed this important report with unrestrained
August 19, 1987

enthusiasm, and 1 urge the federal Government to implement these recommendations at the earliest opportunity.

subsubtopic: CAPE BRETON-UNEMPLOYMENT REDUCED
speechtext:

subsubtopic: EFFECT ON SMALL BUSINESSES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in stage two of its tax reform, the Government wants to introduce a new 8 per cent sales tax that would apply to nearly all goods and services, including food. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has ignored entirely the problems this kind of tax might create for small businesses.
The Canadian Federation of Independent Businesses very accurately described what the impact would be on these businesses. First, the new tax would be an administrative nightmare for all small businesses. Second, small businesses are not in the same position as large companies to pass the cost of the new tax on to the consumer. And third, the new tax will discourage consumption.
Mr. Speaker, 75 per cent of Canadian businesses have an annual turnover of less than $250,000, which is only 5 per cent of total Canadian sales.

speechtext:
