The House resumed from Tuesday, August 18, consideration of the motion of Mr. Bouchard that Bill C-55, an Act to amend the Immigration Act, 1976 and to amend other Acts in consequence thereof, be read a second time and referred to a legislative committee.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday, speaking on the hoist motion, 1 had a chance to express some of the background relating to Bill C-55. I pointed out the changing situation of refugees around the world. We focused on the refugee situation in Europe and Iron Curtain countries after the Second World War. Now the focus tends to be on the Third World. There has been a growth of restrictive measures in western countries so that refugees are having a more difficult time gaining access to all countries in the western world. Instead of refugees being seen as people in need, they are being seen more and more as threats to the status quo. We are taking a very self-centred approach to people who are in the most extreme kinds of need.
I pointed to the unacceptable abuse of our own refugee determination system and the need to improve that, but at the same time we have had the failure of the Conservative Government to take timely action to deal with it. It was presented with the Plaut report. Instead of acting on that, it mandated the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment
and Immigration to study it. When the standing committee presented its report, the Government took no action.
I pointed to the latent racism that exists among Canadians, as, indeed, exists among people all over the world. It lies not too far beneath the surface in most of our lives. Racism is something that needs to be resisted, not catered to. Unfortunately, Bill C-55 and Bill C-84 are catering to a fear of other peoples, a fear of other cultures. It is a kind of xenophobia that is unacceptable for the kind of Canada we want to build in the 1980s and into the 21st century.
Racism has had its time. We should leave it behind and develop the kind of legislation that will lead to a more open society, not one that is more fearful and based on the belief that we have to put up walls in order to protect our values. If we have faith in our values we should be willing to test them in a multicultural society and world.
When the standing committee presented its report in November, 1985, it outlined four basic principles as fundamental to the approach of the committee. I want to read those four principles because I believe they are key to the whole refugee determination process:
1.	It is the Committee's strongly-held conviction that Canadians do not want people sent back to countries where they may be persecuted.
2.	Every person in Canada who wishes to claim that he or she is a Convention refugee should have an unqualified right of access to a formal process that will adjudicate the claim.
3.	All Convention refugee claimants should have their case decided at a non-adversarial oral hearing.
4.	The decision-maker in the formal process shall have the power, in addition to declaring an individual to be a Convention refugee, to recommend to the Minister that specific individuals who are not within the strict definition of Convention refugee, nevertheless should be considered for landing on compassionate and humanitarian grounds.
Those four principles have not been adhered to in Bill C-55.
The committee pointed out that it had been persuaded by Rabbi Plaut and other witnesses that the decision to provide the protection of Canada to those who have well-founded fears of returning to their own country should be undertaken by a body of people knowledgeable and sensitive to human rights issues rather than immigration issues. The determination decision is not an immigration matter, but instead a decision as to who are Convention refugees in need of Canada's protection.
Care must be taken to make sure that our international obligations to Convention refugee claimants are dealt with by a refugee determination system that is not part of our immigration system.
Those are the four principles that the standing committee set out and which, unfortunately, Bill C-55 does not adhere to. The refugee determination system does not follow the general recommendation of the committee.
Rabbi Plaut said, and the committee concurs with him, that declaring a claimant to be a refugee is not a privilege we grant
August 19, 1987

but rather a right we acknowledge. I think it is important for us to think about the meaning of that assertion. We think of citizenship in Canada as a privilege. Certainly those who come as immigrants in the normal stream, coming to Canada is a privilege. However, with respect to those who come as refugees, we say we are recognizing a right rather than granting a privilege.
We recognize this as a right because we, as a nation, have signed certain international covenants. We recognize that we have broad obligations to humanity, broad obligations to our brothers and sisters throughout the world. Where people are in need of refuge, we as a nation that prides itself on a humane tradition, a tradition of fairness and helping those in need, have an obligation to provide that refuge. It is not a privilege we extend but a right that we recognize.
The committee agreed with Rabbi Plaut that there should be no distinction between those who have entered Canada legally and those who have entered illegally when it comes to applying for refugee status. That is, there are those who come to Canada without full documentation and without going through all the procedures. However, the committee said that they should still be entitled to apply for refugee status.
The committee recommended that there should be broad grounds for appeal when refugee status has been denied, and not just on points of law as Bill C-55 provides.
The committee provided for a shorter appeal process. This really is the crux of the abuse of the system. Our appeal process is so long and drawn out that people can take advantage of it. The committee and other people such as Rabbi Plaut have proposed models that would have a much shorter appeal process but would still be fair and would give the benefit of due process to refugee claimants while not allowing them to stay in Canada for up to five years.
These kinds of recommendations would have eliminated the abuses but would also have left a fair system in place. Unfortunately, Bill C-55 is legislation that does not leave a fair system.
I want to point out some of the objections to Bill C-55 that have been raised in a submission by the Montreal Coalition for Refugees. It is a submission that I commend to all Members of Parliament for their study and thought.
The committee states:
-we see as dangerous and unacceptable a proposed system which will govern our borders and yet fails to reach basic human right standards. For instance, the bill requires that the "burden of proof' lies with the claimant. Thus the bill contains a "presumption of abuse" unless the individual, despite his likely initial confusion and distress can prove otherwise.
When people arrive as refugees I think we all recognize that they have been under a great deal of stress. I believe it is not fair to lay upon them the additional stress that they have to prove that they are not abusing the system. The Coalition points to certain moral failures in the Bill. It states:
The denial of a complete hearing is unjust. The practitioners opposing this document know from experience that it is extremely difficult for refugees having just arrived in Canada to immediately (within twenty-four hours)
Immigration Act, 1976
present their claim and expose their reasons. It is more than probable that an adjudicator preoccupied with immigration demands, will not recognize that a person is a refugee at the instant of his arrival.
Yet, such a person will not have a second chance to present his case. Furthermore, the speedy character of the pre-selection process will in practice deny the claimant of the right to counsel of his choice.
Secondly:
The list of "safe third countries" goes against Canada's humanitarian tradition. No country is safe for everyone.
Either we are creating diplomatic difficulties for Canada or we are creating a very unfair system for refugees. If we have a situation where we have to declare, for example, that the United States is an unsafe third country, as it very obviously is for Salvadorans or Guatemalan refugees, we are then creating some diplomatic difficulties between ourselves and the United States. Why are we doing this to ourselves? Why do we not eliminate the possibility of a "safe third country" because there is no such thing.
The Coalition goes on to state:
The pre-selection process for refugee claimants violates international norms of protection.
It points out that Bill C-55 violates the principles of justice upheld in Canada. It states:
Bill C-55 does not in any way reflect the consensus that emerged from Government consultations with, among others, the Canadian Bar Association, Rabbi Gunther Plaut, the churches and non-governmental organizations who continuing to demand:
(i)	universal access to a simple, fair and efficient system
(ii)	an impartial decision making body formed by refugee experts and
chosen in consultation with other concerned organizations.
(iii)	an initial and full hearing
(iv)	the right to a lawyer of one's choice
(v)	a full right of appeal
(vi)	the independence of the refugee system from immigration
(vii)	equitable treatment of claims made abroad.
The Government has never formally rejected these objectives in principle but Bill C-55 denies them.
In conclusion, I would urge the Government to withdraw Bill C-55 and bring in a Bill which would eliminate the abuse, provide for a shorter appeal process, but still provide for a full and fair hearing for refugee claimants so that Canada will continue to be a country that can hold its head high when it looks at the whole refugee situation throughout our world.

speakerposition: Chief Opposition Whip; Whip of the Liberal Party
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the debate on Bill C-55 is important and we are now into our ninth hour of debate in the House. Therefore I am not exaggerating when I say that it is imperative to appreciate fully what is being proposed through Bill C-55 which is aimed

August 19, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
at revamping the refugee determination process and establishing mechanisms-stricter perhaps, and perhaps even more adequate-to be able to decide who is a bona fide refugee.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the Government has had three years to study this important question. It has done precious little during those three years. It came to the House last May 5 and introduced the Bill for first reading. We waited until June 18 to begin second reading of the Bill, a day which, as we recall, was full of other things-that was the day the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) made his famous statement on tax reform. And the Government used Bill C-55 as a kind of filler. Since then, the Government has not seemed too anxious to follow through on Bill C-55. And as Hon. Members are aware, many non-governmental organizations with special expertise in this field have recommended the Government give the Bill a great deal of thought. Mr. Speaker, I welcome this opportunity to take part in the debate because even if we have only 10 minutes each, I will try to get across my personal position on Bill C-55, a Bill that, I admit, has its good points but also contains a number of weaknesses which I think should be corrected in committee. It is important to realize that when, either today or tomorrow, we finish the second reading stage here in the House, the committee that will consider the Bill will, I hope, consider the substantive amendments that are in order.
Mr. Speaker, we have had information from every possible source regarding refugee status determination in Canada. There was a major commission chaired by Rabbi Gunther Plaut and appointed by the Minister of Employment and Immigration at the time, Miss Flora MacDonald, which produced a voluminous report which, I imagine, has been thoroughly examined by Hon. Members and contains a number of recommendations.
I would like to start my comments by reading the report's conclusion which, I think, is particularly important, and I quote from page 215 of the Plaut Report:
I end this report with two observations made by the United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees in the summer of 1984.
The ability to states to respond positively to refugee situations, he said, "depends very largely on a favourable climate of public opinion." He further stressed the unhappy fact that there has been
increasing evidence in recent years of confusion in the public mind between the very special situation of refugees and that of the many millions of other aliens who are endeavouring to gain entry into countries otherthan their own. This confusion has been to the detriment of refugees and has tended to impede a sympathetic approach to refugees at the official level.
I shall go on, because I think this is important. It is not that long.
We in Canada will do well to heed this caution. We need to give urgent attention to promoting a renewed understanding of the special situation of the refugee, and both governmental and non-governmental organizations will wish to co-operate in doing so.
Mr. Speaker, I submit that since the session resumed on August 11, there has been a lot of confusion between, on the
one hand, Bill C-84, a deterrent measure that also provides for the detention of some individuals that enter this country under perhaps special conditions, and the overall immigration question on the other hand. All that has been mixed up, and confused in the minds of Canadians, sometimes by a Government that was not too clear as to its objectives, and that I must recognize, sometimes according to the perceptions and views that we have at least in my constituency of Ottawa-Vanier, wanted to spread confusion by making Canadians believe there was an emergency because of 174 Sikhs who landed in Nova Scotia.
Mr. Speaker, like many other Members I went through the experience of welcoming refugees in Ottawa when the Vietnamese, the boat people faced an emergency situation. At that time, we accepted a significant number; I am told 100,000 Vietnamese were accepted in this country. In my own city, 4,000 were. We put in place systems, mechanisms to help human beings who were going through a crisis. That was the Canadian way. That was absolutely honest and open in my view.
All of a sudden we have 174 people arriving in the middle of the night, under very unique and difficult circumstances, as I mentioned earlier. So a state of crisis is declared and public opinion is fed the idea that the refugee system is subjected to terrible abuse and that immigrants and refugees are one and the same.
I feel that the Government should clarify the situation and that is why I do not hesitate to ask my colleagues in the House to rise and speak to this issue, over which we have debated a mere nine hours, so that Canadians can be made to understand what is at stake here, which is not to make it possible or easy to abuse the system. I would think that all Hon. Members have understood this, as have all Canadians. We are against abuse, we do not want people to break the law and get away with it. But what Bill C-55 is concerned with is the determination of what the refugee status is. This is important since the public does not have a clear idea as to who is an immigrant and who is a refugee. We do not get one hundred thousand of them every year. Barely 20,000 people qualify as refugees every year. It is true that at the present time there are more applications for refugee status than our officials or the system can handle.
A ready solution comes to mind: we need only increase our capacity to handle such applications and put in place a mechanism to deal with them as expeditiously as possible.
Mr. Speaker, the essential merit of Bill C-55 is to allow the number of unprocessed applications for refugee status to be worked down to a manageable level by decreasing the amount of time elapsed between the initial request and its final acceptance or rejection. The idea is to speed up the process to take care of what has been termed the back-log problem.
August 19, 1987

The whole process entails a maximum of three stages: a preselection at the initial hearing stage; a hearing before two members of the Refugee Board; and, as a last resort, an appeal to the Federal Court on legal grounds only, if necessary.
Mr. Speaker, the present mechanism comprises at least seven stages. Their number is thus more than halved under the new procedure. Up until now, the process could stretch over five years, as we well know. It was drawn out, often costly and difficult as well.
The amendments in Bill C-55 would allow for the shortening of the first stage. As I said, that can translate into acceptance or removal.
I could speak for much more than 10 minutes on the flaws of the Bill, because there are many. Indeed, 1 raised the matter a number of times in this debate on the occasion of questions put to Hon. Members. The numerous flaws start with the preselection process, the safe third country approach, the Refugeee Board, the appeal mechanism and the precedent encouraging other countries to take similar steps while claiming they are concerned with the well-being of refugees.
Mr. Speaker, when a claimant appears before the adjudicator and the member of the Refugee Board, under the preselection process, as proposed in Bill C-55, his claim unfortunately is treated according to the country of origin, which jeopardizes the protection that should be afforded to people who claim refugee status.
This is why 1 put the following question to the Conservative Member when he had the floor: How will we determine what is a safe third country? Is the United States a safe third country? They do not accept people from Guatemala. They also refuse to accept people from El Salvador, returning them back home.
So there should be an exact determination of what is a safe country to which we can return an individual, a human being in distress who comes here as a refugee.
Mr. Speaker, this in my view is the work that will have to be accomplished in committee.
I see that you are about to interrupt my comments, Mr. Speaker, and I will conclude on that.
1 know the Government told us they would not return an individual to a country where that individual could be prosecuted or unfairly treated.
But the question that comes to mind is this: If we return an individual to the country of origin, whichever-Holland in the case of Tamils or the United States in the case of someone from Guatemala-Mr. Speaker, this should be determined and 1 feel the committee has an important task to accomplish. It is important in my view that the Bill be reconsidered, and if possible amended in committee. I thank hon. Members for their attention.
Immigration Act, 1976

Mr. Speaker, I am sorry to have to participate in this debate again. I am sorry about what is happening, that the House has met in the middle of August when 1 think Members should be out in their constituencies or taking some time to prepare for the jobs that need to be done when the session gets going again in the fall.
We are here because of an emergency, because of a crisis. But, unfortunately, it seems to me that this is a crisis because of the standing of the Progressive Conservative Party in the polls much more than it is a crisis in terms of a need for instant action on an issue related to refugees on which there have been some solid and constructive proposals put forward by the Standing Committee on Labour, Employment and Immigration, as well as in the report of Rabbi Gunther Plaut of Toronto some two years ago.
If this were a priority the Government could have acted at that time to begin to shorten the very long period of time that it takes for refugee claimants to have their cases adjudicated. Everyone agrees that that time is too long. But I want to address some comments through you, Mr. Speaker, to those citizens who will read this debate or who are perhaps watching the debate today and who are scratching their heads with respect to what has happened.
Certain members of the Conservative Party have cited opinion polls saying that Canadians want action on this particular issue. It is true that if one asks people if something should be done to prevent people trafficking in people who may be false refugees and from dumping them off our coast, most Canadians say yes. We say yes, too. I say yes as a New Democrat. I think what Canadians have to be aware of is that what we have from the Government is, in Gunther Plaut's words, an hysterical over-reaction to a situation, a situation which required change, yes, but not a situation which required the kind of change that we have right now.
I wish to cite and to deplore the comments made by the Minister of Employment and Immigration (Mr. Bouchard) when he appeared before the legislative committee on Bill C-84 yesterday. He accused the churches of having violated immigration law for the past 10 years in terms of the assistance they have given to refugees. He admitted that the Bill which we sent from this place a day or so ago, Bill C-84, does nothing to stop those immigration consultants who were instrumental in bringing in people from Portugal, Turkey and Brazil who, it would appear, were actually false claimants of refugee status and who certainly did not come from countries which have generated large numbers of refugees in the past.
Yet the Bill which the Government put forward in response to what it says is a crisis and an emergency did nothing to impose penalties on these consultants who have, I believe, in seeking to abuse our laws in the process, abused the generosity that most Canadians feel in helping people who are genuinely

August 19, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
in fear, in legitimate fear of persecution in their home countries. None of those consultants involved with the Portuguese and the other groups that came have in fact been prosecuted.
One asks, if the Minister or the Government wanted to send a signal, why has that kind of signal not been sent and why are there no proposals today to change the penalties from what existed before?
1 believe that Canadians are being given a wrong picture in terms of the refugee situation as a consequence of the landing of a group of Sikhs off the shores of Nova Scotia. Some 17,000 people have sought refugee status this year. Some 174 additional ones coming in is equivalent to an extra 1 per cent. It is a very small number. The only previous time we have had a similar incident was when the Tamils came in one year ago. I remind Canadians that at that time the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) himself welcomed that group of Tamils and said, "We will do our best to ensure that you are seriously considered for the refugee status you seek", despite the curious circumstances under which they were brought to Canada's shores.
Last year that was okay; this year it is not. I believe that the Government and members of the Government are trying to place in peoples' minds an impression that hordes-very large numbers-of dark-skinned applicants for refugee status are coming to Canada.
MO)
The Government has taken different sides in this issue, and perhaps it is seeking to exploit fears relating to internal politics in India where there are tensions between the Sikh and Hindu populations. Because Sikhs wear turbans and look different, it is being suggested that there is something wrong with Sikhs being here in Canada. Canada has 150,000 Sikhs. The vast majority, like the vast majority of immigrants from every country, make a solid and constructive contribution, regardless of the national or religious dress they choose to wear.
Every person seeking or applying for refugee status is not necessarily a legitimate refugee. That is not the question. The question is whether somebody who is seeking refugee status has a reasonable case to be there. The figures this year indicate that of the 17,000 people who have applied 4,000 came from El Salvador. That country has a history of death squads and dictatorship that has continued despite the election of the government under President Napoleon Duarte which was going to clean things up. The serious problems there are exacerbated by the meddling of the Central Intelligence Agency, and of the Americans in Central America where their shenanigans have extended beyond Nicaragua to other countries in that region.
A further 1,208 applicants came from Guatemala. The same situation prevails in that country. Hundreds of thousands of people have become displaced, stateless, or forced into refugee
status in Central America because of political disturbances, and state terrorism in those areas.
One thousand six hundred and eighty-seven applicants came from Sri Lanka. I would hope that the recent agreement between Prime Minister Ghandi and the President of Sri Lanka regarding the status of the Tamils and the decentralization of power to the northern states in Sri Lanka will lead to a settling of the grievances of the Tamil population, and of the problems which have created refugees. In the past, Canada has accepted a number of Tamils as refugees. One has to assume that a number of the people from Sri Lanka were legitimately seeking refuge because of their Tamil origins, and their legitimate fear of persecution, oppression, or death.
One thousand six hundred and fifty-two people were seeking refugee status from Iran. I need not comment on the situation in Iran, and what has been done to the people of the Baha'i religion, or those deemed to be enemies of the ruling religious regime in Iran.
One thousand two hundred and ninety people have applied from Chile where the Pinochet dictatorship continues. This weekend I read the devastating novel by Isabel Allende, the niece of the former President, Salvador Allende. In her novel she describes the events that took place there, and the degree to which the Conservative right wing in Chile were disillusioned, and deeply disturbed and distressed by the manner in which their country literally went to the dogs during the takeover by the military at the time that President Allende was murdered, and the democratically elected progressive Government was defeated. Certainly, Chileans have a legitimate case to argue that they are suffering fear of political persecution.
Of the top six refugee applicant producing countries, the only one which we might question would be Brazil. It produced 1,681 applicants. I am not qualified to judge whether or not those applicants are genuine.
We have to bear in mind that out of total immigration this year of approximately 120,000, there was a relatively small number of people seeking to have their refugee claims dealt with fairly. I believe this total should be increased. The other day in the House the Minister announced that this total will be increased because of a relaxation of the family reunification policies.
Churches, refugee aid groups, the Canadian Bar Association, and other groups, have put forward constructive proposals to accelerate the consideration of refugee status claims. At the same time, they have stated solidly that they believe that Bill C-55 is wrong. In particular, they feel that it is wrong for Canada to have a situation in place where applicants for refugee status can be turned away at the border because of an administrative determination taken within 72 hours that they have touched down on a safe country on the way to Canada.
People who have come from Sri Lanka, El Salvador, Iran, Chile, Afghanistan, and other countries generating refugee applicants can hardly help but pass through another country.
August 19, 1987

Bill C-55 effectively gives these quick tribunals at the border the authority to turn away most applicants for refugee status, without any serious look at whether their claims are valid. 1 do not believe that is in the spirit of Canadians.
Most Canadians feel it is wrong when our Minister of Employment and Immigration suggests that the churches, and other refugee groups working out of charity and generosity are breaking the law, and should continue to live under the threat that they may be prosecuted for continuing to break the law. Surely, that is wrong. That is one of the reasons why I believe that Bill C-55 should be opposed. Instead, Canada should put in place recommendations and proposals along the lines of those put forward to accelerate the process without victimizing persons who seek refugee status.

Mr. Speaker, it is an unhappy reality that the House of Commons is still debating Bill C-55 in principle. I had hoped that the Bill would either have been delayed for six months by the vote yesterday, or withdrawn by the Government. There has been extremely cogent and detailed criticism of the gross inadequacies in the Bill, and the serious dangers to our tradition as a humanitarian country open to immigrants and refugees. Those people have made a tremendous contribution to our country. Instead, this piece of legislation is still in front of us.
The Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops described this proposed legislation in the following terms:
This proposed legislation and its objective go against the humanitarian traditions of the people of this country, who in great majority are descendants of immigrants and/or refugees.
Yet, the Bill is still in front of us, and the Government persists, despite the fact that there are three fundamental faults that are self-evident to anyone who has looked through the legislation with any care.
First, the procedure for refugees which is established by this Bill makes our country inaccessible to a great many people who would like to be able to claim at least the chance for a hearing. They are not claiming the right to settle here, but the right to a hearing. Instead of ensuring that everyone can have their claim heard, this Bill sets up a system which I predict will eliminate the chances of 75 to 80 per cent of those who come to our borders seeking to have their claims heard. That means that 75 per cent to 80 per cent will not even have the opportunity of a hearing.
Second, there is a basic contradiction of the notion that those who judge claims should be independent of those who are regulating the system.
Let me quote from the news release of the Inter-Church Committee for Refugees:
Instead of providing an independent procedure specialized in refugee determination and related international law, this legislation relies on decisionmakers operating in an immigration control environment who have shown little understanding of standards of justice or human rights,-
Immigration Act, 1976
Finally, there is within this legislation no meaningful appeal. Instead of allowing access to a specialized independent appeal body, the legislation seeks to use the Federal Court in an inappropriate and unworkable way. It permits rights of appeal only on points of law, not on the merits of the case, which in itself is a further movement away from the traditions of justice as we have known them in Canada.
The legislation, as the Inter-Church Committee says, represents no improvement on the proposals of May 21, 1986 which were condemned at the Canadian Council for Refugees meeting that followed the announcement of that initiative. Of course the most recent Canadian Council for Refugees meeting was even more scathing in respect of the injustice and unfairness within the legislation.
If one had a choice between this and the previous legislation and nothing else-if that was the choice before us-one might well have to look at some parts of the Bill which are at least an improvement over the incredibly lengthy, unfair, and completely inadequate systems of refugee determination we presently have. However, an alternative has been presented by the Canadian Council of Churches. It is an alternative that sets out five stages through which refugee determination would take place.
The first stage would be a simple arrival stage with the refugee claimant arriving at the border and immigration officials registering the person and referring the person to a refugee board. At that point we would not have the principle of refugees being returnable, accepted by legislation, as this piece of legislation would do.
Stage two would be the stage at which the refugee himself makes an appointment with the refugee board for an oral hearing within a fixed time period after the referral has taken place.
Stage three would be the oral hearing itself at which the claimant and an independent legal counsel the claimant would be able to obtain, rather than a duty counsel, as is the case in the present legislation, would present the case to a two-person panel of competent, specialized persons on a refugee board who would decide whether or not they believe the person is a refugee.
If at that stage the answer from the refugee board is no, there would be an appeal review stage at which unsuccessful claimants could submit additional information for a paper review, as the Council of Churches puts it, by a specialized level of the independent refugee board within a fixed time of receipt of reasons for refusal in the context of a transcript being available. At that stage the appeal body could overrule a negative decision or request a rehearing. The Council of Churches suggests that this would take a maximum of about 14 weeks, which is far less than the present system.
Finally, there would be the potential for appeal to the Federal Court on points of law, because an appeal would already have taken place on substantive issues. It is suggested

August 19, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
by the Council of Churches that that would require four weeks to thirteen weeks. Therefore, the maximum amount of time we could be talking about would be 27 weeks for a full, fair, and effective review procedure.
That is the alternative which exists. That is why the approach by the Government is so unfair and so unjust and will ultimately be part of what brings the Government down when an election is finally called.

Mr. Speaker, every poll which has been taken has indicated to us as Members of Parliament that the people of Canada are very sympathetic to a policy permitting a substantial number of legitimate refugees to come to Canada. What they are opposed to is people who are not really refugees being permitted to come here. They are opposed to people who may be refugees jumping to the head of the line, as did the Tamils who came here a year ago, were welcomed by the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), and were assured that Canada would always be generous to refugees who came here. They are also opposed to the recent entry of Sikhs into Canada by boat.
What they want is a fair and humane system. When the Government says that the people support what it is proposing, it is right, except it has not explained to ordinary Canadians what this Bill really means.
People who are interested in and supportive of helping refugees come to Canada, such as Amnesty International, the Canadian Labour Congress, the Canadian Jewish Congress, the Ethno-Cultural Council, and the major churches, having looked at the legislation and thought through its implications and the power it gives to Government and to officials of various Departments, have unanimously expressed opposition to it.
Let me quote a couple of lines from a telex sent to the Prime Minister on June 1 of this year on behalf of 11 major church groups in Canada. In part it reads:
We urge you and your government to replace Bill C-55 with legislation which provides:
-access for all claimants to a full, fair and independent hearing,
-a meaningful appeal.
Then it went on to indicate:
The Bill is being promoted on the false premise that it will protect genuine refugees. It is clear that the effect of the Bill, with a preliminary hearing which is no more than an elaborate mechanical screening, and with no meaningful appeals, will be to turn away genuine refugees. In addition, the provisions of this Bill undermine rights and standards of justice in Canada for everyone.
Also Members of Parliament received a letter from the General Secretary of the Canadian Conference of Catholic Bishops dated June 11 of this year, in which the following was indicated:
This proposed legislation and its objective go against the humanitarian traditions of the people of this country, who in great majority are descendants of immigrants and/or refugees.
Let us look at the powers this Bill gives to the Government and the people who work for the Government. Allan Borovoy, the leading activist for the Canadian Civil Liberties Association and a very prominent lawyer has said:
Almost every section violates some fundamental principle of civil liberties and democracy.
He is talking about Bill C-55.
Let us look at the analysis of this Bill of the Manitoba Bar Association, as reported by The Toronto Star. Bill C-84 would allow officials to do the following:
Detain people without documents for seven days without higher authorization.
Extend detention for another 21 days with a Minister's certificate.
Keep undocumented claimants in detention indefinitely if an adjudicator agrees the Government is making reasonable efforts to track down their identity. After the first 28 days of detention, the case will be reviewed every seven days-
Make an arbitrary decision on who is or is not a security threat, based on any evidence the Government wishes to consider.
If I can digress for a moment, one can imagine the kind of security advice on potential refugees one would receive from the Governments of Chile, El Salvador or some Communist countries.
The Bill will permit the Government to do the following:
Lock up people earmarked for deportation until a federal court hearing is set.
Bar the suspect and his lawyer from seeing the complete evidence against him if the Canadian Security and Intelligence Service or RCMP classifies it as secret.
Bar the court from seeing the complete evidence for similar reasons.
Imagine a Canadian law which would bar a judge from seeing evidence in a case with which he is dealing. That is a disgraceful proposal.
The analysis continues by indicating that the Bill would do the following:
Deny appeal to anybody judged a security risk by the court-though Canadian law grants the right of appeal to those convicted of crimes. (Lawyers say it may be possible to retain right of appeal through court procedures).
Deport those considered security risks as soon as possible.
Remove the right of those apprehended as security risks to a review of the evidence of their case by the Security and Intelligence Review Committee.
The article goes on to say:
If immigration officials or police are on the trail of illegal immigrants or a smuggling racket, Bill C-84 gives them sweeping powers to search homes, offices, property or vehicles that will supply evidence if a justice of the peace signs a certificate.
We know how quickly justices of the peace or judges will sign any certificate asked for by the police.
The article goes on:
According to the Government, the powers are needed to apprehend criminals and avoid destruction of evidence. But lawyers, including the Manitoba Bar Association, say the legislation goes farther than the powerful narcotics laws.
August 19, 1987

I for one know that the Manitoba Bar Association is not a very radical organization, to say the least.
The article continues by saying that the Bill would also allow the following:
Search of property in any part of the country, even if the original warrant is issued in another province.
Search of private homes where landlords rent space to non-Canadian tenants, if immigration officials suspect they are illegal immigrants.
Forcible search of property including smashing doors, windows, locks, floors, ceilings, walls or anything deemed necessary by immigration officers or police if they suspect evidence will be destroyed.
Search and seizure without warrant if "by reason of exigent circumstances it would not be practical to obtain the warrant."
Confiscation of any property officials or police think necessary.
I do not think that a Communist country like the Soviet Union would possibly give its police any more power than this Bill gives immigration officials and RCMP officers.
It is not surprising that all those groups and organizations to which I referred oppose this Bill. It is not surprising that Manitobans to whom I have spoken in the last few days including Mennonites, Roman Catholics, Anglicans and members of the United Church who have been helping refugees have told me in very clear and unequivocal terms that if the things which they have done in the past and which they continue to do in the future to help refugees settle in Canada will violate this law when it is passed, they are prepared to suffer the consequences. If they are arrested, charged, tried and sentenced by a court, they are prepared to pay the penalty.
It is a sad day for Canada when people who want to do the right thing, the humanitarian thing, are told that if they continue to do so they may indeed wind up in jail. As members of my Party, I have no intention of supporting this Bill as it is drafted at the present time. We will do everything we can to oppose the passage and implementation of this Bill.

Mr. Speaker, Canada has a very long tradition of welcoming refugees fleeing from persecution. In fact, it accepted some 37,000 Hungarians in the mid-fifties, some 12,000 Czechs in the late sixties, some 7,000 Ugandans in 1972, some 700 Cypriots in 1975 and nearly 10,000 Vietnamese in 1975, 1976 and 1977, and quite recently, early in the 1980s, some 9,000 Poles.
It should be emphasized that this reputation has also made it possible for us to accept a few thousand other refugees from Iran, El Salvador, Lebanon, Sri Lanka and Guatemala more recently. Altogether, when we add up all these new Canadians, we find that we have accepted some 360,000 refugees since 1950, or an average of 12,000 people a year.
In view of the size of Canada, opening our door every year to some 12,000 people who live under difficult and painful circumstances and who are sometimes persecuted in countries where freedom does not exist quite as much as here is nothing to write home about. There is certainly plenty of room for them in Canada. In fact, our country was awarded the
Immigration Act, 1976
prestigious Nansen Medal by the United Nations in recognition of our action in favour of the needy. It should be emphasized that this medal was awarded to the Canadian Government, both present and past, but above all to the Canadian people who have always very well accepted these people who are in need and difficulty. We would have felt that this Conservative Government would have been anxious to maintain this generous and welcoming attitude towards these unfortunate people in search of a new country.
In fact, the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) had stated when the Tamils arrived in August, 1986, that if the scale were to tilt, it would on the side of compassion and justice. Well, Mr. Speaker, we simply cannot understand the attitude of the Conservative Government which has now introduced a series of legislation that go squarely against this spirit of generosity and good will that has always characterized Canada.
To want to limit the flow of false refugee claimants to Canada is legitimate and something we can accept and support. But the measures announced by the Government go far beyond that and are aimed at closing the door on many refugee claimants who arrive in Canada, and not at changing the refugee determination process.
As the Leader of the Liberal Opposition (Mr. Turner) was saying, in order to stop the queue-jumpers, the Conservative Government has decided to close the theatre. Instead of telling these people who do not want to wait their turn to please go back and wait in line, the Conservative Government has decided to penalize everybody and shut the door. It is an unacceptable and incomprehensible attitude which we denounce.
I should like to quote from an editorial by Pierre Venat which appeared in La Presse under the heading: "A Bill that needs to be amended". "The Bill, which minister Bouchard introduced last week for the purpose of strengthening the Canadian legislation on immigration, does not deserve to be adopted unless it is thoroughly amended."
Even the Hon. Member for La Prairie (Mr. Jourdenais) who belongs to the Progressive Conservative Party, shares this view.
There can be no doubt that people are ill at ease when they see this flood of foreign citizens whose customs and habits are sometimes altogether different from their own-"
But a number of people simply do not know what to make of the Government's approach to this problem, and indeed it ought to be reconsidered. This is the view of Montreal's Coalition pour les refugies, the Canadian Bar, Amnesty International, and the Civil Liberties Union-they all want the Bill to be amended. As it happens, the Liberal Party of Canada has unequivocally expressed its concerns about the Bill, and I will recall them very briefly.
First, we believe that the prescreening mechanism builds a wall around the system we seek to improve. In a way the Government washes its hands of the refugee problem, leaving

August 19, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
other countries to deal with it. As we see it, this Pontius Pilate attitude is unacceptable.
Second, we believe that the prescreening procedure creates more problems than it solves. Why confuse the two issues of immigration and refugees when in fact the purpose of the whole exercise is to make a distinction between the two.
Every year, there are thousands of Canadians across this country who want to bring their relatives to Canada. These are people who emigrated to Canada from various other countries. They are happy in their new country and they want to bring their mother or brothers or a cousin over to join them in Canada and live in this beautiful country of ours.
The family reunification policy, which has always been the cornerstone of the Liberal Party's immigration policy when it was in power, is now being maliciously undermined by a Conservative Government that wants to close the door to immigration. It is using the fact that a couple of people wanted to jump the queue as an excuse to impose new immigration criteria in Canada that will destroy not only the open policy we have always had with respect to refugees but also the policy maintained vis-a-vis those who want to bring relatives over to Canada.
1 have no hesitation in saying that the Government's policy will be disastrous not only for refugees who absolutely must find a new country but also for Canada's family reunification policy which should be permanent.
Canadians of many origins have made extraordinary contributions to this country. They have enriched our culture and are now living happily and in harmony with other Canadians, and they have the right to hope that their family members will be able to join them in this country. We believe this Bill may actually diminish their chances of family reunification.
That is why we do not like this Bill and why we, the Liberal Party of Canada, intend to vote against this measure which in the circumstances, we feel, is excessive just to deal with a minor problem. To amend legislation, the Government is using a sledge hammer. To end certain abuses that are easy to control, the Government is closing our doors to many people who normally would have been able to enter Canada to join our growing Canadian labour force. We believe the Government is on the wrong track with this poorly prepared, poorly drafted and philosophically unsound legislation.
Mr. Speaker, I do not know if the Hon. Minister is applauding the last speech or my introduction.

speakerposition: Minister of Public Works; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
speechtext: Both.

Thank you.
1 am pleased to rise and speak in the debate on Bill C-55. As you know, we are considering two immigration Bills, this one and Bill C-84 which is now in committee. We were called back into emergency session because the Government decided a crisis situation existed, and the first Bill tabled was C-84. I spoke on that Bill on the first day, Tuesday, August 11, as recorded at page 7955 of Hansard.
I do not want to repeat my remarks, but I did acknowledge there was tremendous public pressure, to judge by the telephone calls and letters we received at our constituency offices, to act to change what was considered an unfair process. People were coming in as refugees and using the process to stay in Canada for two, three, four or five years. At the same time legitimate immigrants could not get into the country at all. Obviously something had to be done.
During my speech I said I thought if we could sum up the public's attitude it was to let the real refugees in, because we are bound by the UN Convention we signed, and throw the phoney ones out. We must have a fair procedure to do that. Canadians are fair people and are prepared to deal with the matter in a fair way. I thought the Government was going to do that.
I watched the CBC's Journal last night. In my speech of a few days ago I warned about an overkill, that the Government might over-react to this matter. Sure enough, on the Journal was a woman, a grandmother, who was helping legitimate refugees from Central America. She now expresses the fear that due to the Government's Bill C-84 she could be locked up for assisting these refugees. A nun came on after that and said that she too could be locked up for bringing people into Canada without papers, as she has been doing. Legitimate refugees do not have any papers. They flee for their lives and only their lives, literally, not with their papers.
The Government now has itself in a position in which it is putting grandmothers and nuns in jail. Can the Mulroney Government not do anything right? It is going to put grandmothers and nuns in prison for helping refugees? I suggest to the Minister, who is a reasonable man, that he bring in a reasoned amendment to clear up that situation. Members can read the Bill. I am a lawyer and can read the law. There are other lawyers in the House. It is quite plain that under this Bill the grandmothers and nuns would go to jail.
You should be put in jail for talking like that.

The Member wants to put me in jail. He is a typical Conservative. They want to put everyone in jail to solve the problem.
I would like to deal with Bill C-55. Since I have already expressed many of my own views on the matter, in the time I have left I would like to read into the record and make comments on a letter from Amnesty International to the Prime
August 19, 1987

Minister (Mr. Mulroney) dated August 7, 1987. As you know, Mr. Speaker, Amnesty International won the Nobel prize for the peaceful work it has done on behalf of people locked up in jails all over the world. Amnesty International says:
As you may be aware, Amnesty International opposes the forcible return of persons to countries where they may reasonably be expected to be arbitrarily detained for the non-violent expression of their beliefs, tortured or executed. A law which increases the likelihood of such events occurring is therefore of great concern to our organization.
Before outlining some of Amnesty International's concerns about the legislation itself, we wish to address the process of consultation which took place prior to the introduction of the Bill. Non-governmental organizations working with refugees were unanimous in recommending that a new refugee determination procedure embody the principles of universal access, an independent decision-making process, and an appeal on the merits. These principles were also reflected in the recommendations made by the Standing Committee in Labour, Employment and Immigration. Regrettably these recommendations were ignored by Cabinet in proposing this Bill.
Indeed, if the Cabinet had acted sooner and responded to the recommendations of the committee of this House, we would not have had to come back for this special session and would not have had the recent problem which we did with the boat coming in.
The letter continues:
The Bill itself is an attempt to prevent abuse of the determination procedure while at the same time ensuring that genuine refugees will not be returned to countries where their fear of persecution is well-founded. Amnesty shares these concerns.
So do we in the New Democratic Party, Mr. Speaker, and we can agree with the principles which the Government has put in this Bill.
The letter continues:
As we have stated many times in the past, abuse of the process has a detrimental effect upon legitimate claimants.
In fact, we urged your government to impose, long before any action was taken, a visa restriction on Portugal, whose citizens were clogging the system with fraudulent claims.
A lot of people have been afraid to say that in the House of Commons but it needs to be said. There were a lot of fraudulent refugee claims from people from Portugal. They should have been immigrants. If we had a decent and fair procedure for immigrants we might not have had those phoney refugee claims.
Amnesty says:
We therefore support legislation which attempts to curb abuse. However, in its zeal to prevent abuse. Cabinet has seriously undermined the very objective which should be the cornerstone of any law dealing with refugee determination-the protection of genuine refugees.
In our view, the major deficiencies of Bill C-55 lie in its restriction of access, the limited right of appeal and non-independent decision-making. The details of our concerns can be found under the following categories:
(1) Eligibility Criteria
Under Bill C-55 certain refugee claimants are considered ineligible to have a full hearing of their claims on the merits. Five classes of claimants will be excluded from the determination process at a very early stage of the inquiry. Of these, the greatest number will be found ineligible because they have come to Canada from a country which has been prescribed as a "safe third country".
Immigration Act, 1976
I do not have time to read the whole letter so I will summarize it. Amnesty goes on to say that we could get into real trouble with this. For example, if we return Guatemalan and Salvadoran claimants to the United States, a so-called safe third country, they may be sent back to their countries. The Government is then faced with a difficult dilemma. Does it say that the United States, our friend and ally, is not a safe third country? That is a very sticky wicket. I can see what Amnesty is getting at.
They talk about a credible basis test and about who should be making the determination. They talk about a limited right of appeal and the problem of not having full appeals.
We have suggested that there could be a fair appeal process in a much shorter period of time. Amnesty talks about the difficulties of appealing on the law, having an appeal on a legal point, rather than on fact, which is the real basis of determining whether someone is a legitimate refugee. Amnesty concludes by saying:
We reiterate our concern about preventing abuse of the refugee determination process. However, fundamental safeguards are necessary to ensure that genuine refugees will not be returned to face persecution. The life or liberty of one bona fide refugee lost as a result of Canada's restrictive refugee policy would be enough to render such policy a failure. We urge you and your government to amend or withdraw and replace Bill C-55 with legislation which incorporates the fundamental principles of universal access, an appeal on the merits and independent decision-making.
Remember, Mr. Speaker, that this country once returned a boatful of Jewish people and some of those people died as a result. That is a bad blot on our history. None of us want that to be repeated. We all want to make this a fair process. I urge the Minister to study this in committee and make the proper amendments so that there will be proper legal procedure. We will co-operate with the Government on that. However, do not over-react again and get into the position of sending grandmothers and nuns to jail through an overkill process.

Mr. Speaker, I am glad to see that the Minister is in the House. I intend to concentrate on a couple of concerns I have with the situation in which the Government has put us, by recalling Parliament and asking us to deal with this very complicated matter in a somewhat hurried fashion.
I begin by questioning whether or not there is in fact a genuine emergency. I do not think there is an emergency with respect to Canada's refugee policy, certainly not a situation which is so much of a crisis that we could not have been permitted the ordinary parliamentary time for dealing with this very difficult matter. I suspect, without imputing motives to the Minister, who may be acting only on instructions, that there was a political emergency with respect to the Government's own popularity. This is a very cynical, and I think unsuccessful, attempt to take advantage of a great deal of popular concern, in many respects legitimate concerns of the Canadian people with respect to the abuse of Canada's open attitude toward refugees and Canada's refugee policy. Unfortunately, the legislation before us and Bill C-84 which is

August 19, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
now in committee would not deal with the most serious abuses of that system. The Hon. Member for Spadina (Mr. Heap) pointed out on numerous occasions that the Bill would not deal with the people who arrived from Brazil, Portugal and Turkey on registered airline flights with the documentation and everything else they needed. Instead, the Bill is written in such a way that rather than dealing with such obvious abuses it may put at risk genuine refugees.
One element of almost all religious traditions, from as long ago as antiquity, is that a human community is to be judged largely by the way it treats strangers. The Hon. Member for Surrey-White Rock-North Delta (Mr. Friesen) is here and 1 recall saying this with his approval and the approval of other Canadian members of the delegation to the meeting of the Interparliamentary Union in East Berlin in September, 1980. 1 spoke on behalf of the Canadian delegation with respect to refugee concerns that were being debated at that time.
I noted that refugee policy was traditionally one of the moral measures by which the quality of a particular country could be judged. I say that because I want people to understand that Canada's soul is at stake in this debate. Our refugee policy will say a lot about what kind of country we are.
Let me move to two concerns which I believe the Minister can address. Obviously, the Government and the Opposition will continue to have legitimate differences about a number of provisions in this Bill. However, it seems to me that there are two improvements to the legislation that would at least meet the following concerns. Church groups and others have quite properly raised a concern that the measures the Government wants to establish will not only catch people who are deliberately abusing the system for profit but will also make lawbreakers out of those who help others who do not have documents come into the country in the genuine belief that these people are refugees.
The Minister knows that there is quite a difference between someone in Manitoba who drives to Grand Forks to pick up a person whom he believes to be a legitimate refugee from Central America and takes that person directly to an immigration officer in Emerson in the personal, conscientious belief that this person has a claim to refugee status that will stand the test of Canada's determination process even though that person does not have papers, the Minister knows that there is a significant difference between that case and the abuses that the Minister quite rightly wants to stop.
I have not heard the Government make a convincing denial to our belief that the measures the Government wants to introduce do not make any distinction between that person in Manitoba and those who can be convincingly accused of abusing the system. We have suggested some ways in which the Government can change the legislation to meet that concern. I believe that on the basis of simple political advice,
such a change would certainly overcome many of the objections that have been raised with respect to what the Government wants to implement.
Second, in no way should anything we do with respect to refugee policy, either in Bill C-55 or Bill C-84, be seen to be in breach of our international obligations. There was some foo fa raw in the House earlier today about whether our Ambassador to the United Nations was taken out of context with respect to his comments about the Bill. Leaving that debate aside, the fact is that the Ambassador spoke about the possibility of the Bill being made compatible with our international covenants. While that suggests that the Bill in its present form does not meet international covenants, it also suggests that there is a willingness on the part of the Government to attempt to find a way to make the legislation compatible. 1 believe that is very important.
When I had the opportunity to speak in an international forum on refugee policy, I was pleased to be able to get up as a Canadian, knowing that Canada had a certain credibility, not just in practical terms, but in terms of the respect it had shown for the United Nations High Commission for Refugees and other concerns. I ask the Minister to consider the price we will pay for being open to the accusation of being in violation of UN and other international agreements with respect to refugees. Whether the Minister believes that to be the case or not, 1 ask him to consider the price we will pay even if we are perceived to be in violation of those agreements.
1 believe much is at stake. One of the most important roles that Canada plays, not only with respect to refugees but other issues, is our honest broker role, a country with credibility in a great many humanitarian issues. I would hate to see that credibility put at risk.
1 urge the Government to at least find a way to change these Bills with respect to refugee policy even if it insists on being consistent with its other objectives, so that Canada will not be open to those accusations.
I hope the Minister will take these two suggestions to heart because they are two areas in which 1 believe movement is possible on the part of the Government.
I will not even attempt to deal with the larger debate because 1 do not believe 1 have enough expertise. However, I have paid attention to those two issues because they struck me as two glaring weaknesses in the Government's position. I hope the Minister will carefully consider correcting the legislation, and 1 look forward to the Government actually making some changes in that direction.

Mr. Speaker, 1 welcome the opportunity to say a few words on Bill C-55. All Members have received letters, correspondence, and telephone calls from concerned Canadians who want to make sure that our refugee and immigration policy has integrity. I certainly do not question much of the concern that has been expressed to me by individuals who have called or written. However, the question



*

August 19, 1987

that 1 and many other Canadians are asking is whether the Government's response to this kind of problem is not too harsh or extreme.
There are other Canadians who certainly have another point of view. They arrived at their position in an equally honest manner, as individuals who are expressing concern on the other side of the question.
1 am glad to have this opportunity to advise the House that I received a letter today from a constituent. I am quite sure she would not have any objection to her name being mentioned. Her name is Jill McNall. She has written two letters to the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) expressing her point of view on Canada's refugee policy and her concern that this Government is attempting to change that policy. I am sure Hon. Members in the House will be interested to hear what this constituent has to say, so 1 will read her letter as my contribution to this debate. She begins, and I quote:
Dear Prime Minister,
Further to my letter to you in February, 1987, 1 am again writing to express my grave concern about the direction of Canada's refugee policy.
As I indicated in my letter, I was most disturbed by the policies which were imposed in February, 1987, but the introduction of Bill C-55 to the Legislature has left me truly appalled. I feel we are reverting to attitudes and practices which I had hoped we had left behind forever: practices reminiscent of government-sanctioned racism and of the refoulement of Jewish refugees in the Second World War.
1 recognize and appreciate that there have been abuses of our refugee determination process in the past, however, those abuses have largely stemmed from an inappropriate process.
Numerous humane alternative procedures have been suggested in the past which would enable us to deal quickly and fairly with each refugee claimant. A quick procedure is essential to the prevention of abuse of the system. However, a quick procedure which jeopardizes genuine refugees in favour of preventing abuse is completely inappropriate and unacceptable in a country which has prided itself on its assistance to refugees. Bill C-55 will eliminate many refugee claimants in the very early stages of the process before they have even had a chance to tell their own story or to have their own claim judged on its merits.
Refugee claimants are people fleeing from persecution in their native countries, hoping to be given an opportunity to start a new life. They arrive frightened and tired, often speaking very little or no English, and usually with only a minimal idea of what life in Canada is, let alone what our immigration and refugee policy is or how it all works.
The expectation that refugee claimants can be given a fair chance in three to seven days is absurd. Many will not even know that they should indicate their desire to claim refugee status immediately, and they will certainly not have time to get independent advice or counsel.
A great area of concern is also the so-called "safe third country" to which refugee claimants can be returned. These countries will be designated by Cabinet, and I ask myself what factors will be considered? In view of our political ties to the United States for example, how likely is it that the United States could be determined to be a "safe country" for Guatemalan and El Salvadoran refugee claimants, even though virtually all refugee claims from those countries are denied in the United States. This imposition of political considerations on Canada's refugee policy would seriously undermine the integrity of the system.
The right of appeal is a cornerstone of Canadian law, even $500 claim in Small Claim's Court has the right of appeal, yet we would deny that right to people whose lives may be at stake. Bill C-55 drastically restricts the grounds of appeal basically to points of law rather than fact, yet refugee claims are based on fact and credibility. Another reason for the right of appeal is that
Immigration Act, 1976
mistakes happen in any system, and an appeal is a tool for correcting those mistakes. A meaningful right of appeal should be a cornerstone of any policy, but especially where life and liberty may hang in the balance.
Ms. McNall goes on to state:
One of the unfortunate circumstances in this issue is the lack of accurate and up-to-date information available to the general public. I am very concerned by the confusing, often biased, and frequently inaccurate media coverage of matters relating to refugees and immigrants, as the media acts as major source of information for a large number of Canadians. A lot has been said about public opinion being opposed to a so-called "open door" policy, but l believe that, with an accurate information, the majority of Canadians would recognize that refugees are not immigrants or queue-jumpers.
It is difficult for most of us to really understand the plight of refugees, because we were born here or came by choice. It is almost impossible for us to imagine living in fear of our own Government. Refugees are people seeking asylum because of persecution; people who want a chance to start a new life in freedom; people who are willing to work hard and to become contributing members of Canadian society.
In conclusion, I would like to request that Bill C-55 be discarded as an inappropriate and wholly unacceptable solution to a grave and potentially life-threatening concern. Safe, quick and humane alternatives have already been suggested in the past.
I will stop there because 1 feel that Ms. McNall has made her argument, which 1 consider to be one of the best I have heard. This is someone who I do not think has a legal background or any expertise in immigration or refugee matters. She is a person who is speaking from the heart as a decent Canadian. We have always had a decent attitude towards those in other countries who wanted to come here to live within our civilized Canadian society.
If this Government had really wanted to do something about illegal refugees, as it likes to call them, or an immigration system which plainly does not seem to be working as well as it should, why did the Government not act six months ago when it was aware of these problems rather than waiting until a perceived emergency existed? I will tell you why, Mr. Speaker, in my opinion. The Government jumped in because it saw this as being a politically opportune time to respond to a feeling in society towards which it has contributed. If the Government had wanted to go after the smugglers rather than the people being smuggled, I do not believe anyone would have any objection. If it had gone after the individuals who exploited disadvantaged peoples like the Sikhs who came in a month ago, we would have supported it. However, rather than go after the smugglers, it has gone after the people being smuggled and I think the Government should be ashamed of itself for lending its support to that kind of attitude.
Mir. Rod Murphy (Churchill): Mr. Speaker, I only intend to speak for a few minutes on this legislation at this particular stage. I have a number of concerns about Bill C-55, some of which 1 expressed yesterday in a speech I gave on the hoist motion. In that particular speech I pointed out that I do not believe the Government's intent with respect to this legislation is very honourable.
Bill C-55 is a piece of legislation which the Government sat on for three years. The Government has had the advice of the parliamentary committee in which representatives of all three

August 19, 1987
Immigration Act, 1976
Parties indicated they wanted reform of the refugee legislation which would ensure that we keep out those people who are not honest refugees. At the same time, we want a fair system, a system which allows for an appeal process and a system of which Canadians right across this land could be proud. That is what the standing committee of the House of Commons pushed for and that is what we believe should be the basis of the legislation before us. However, that is not the case.
In addition, after stalling for three years, the Government has introduced legislation which is unfair. It is a blight on Canada's reputation. We now have a Government which wants to rush through consideration of this legislation and is insisting that this legislation be passed in all stages prior to the adjournment of this special session of the House.
I think that does not speak well of the Government, not only in that the legislation itself is flawed but in that it is complicated. For the Government to want to rush through this legislation at this time in the middle of summer indicates that it has a political agenda as opposed to a legislative one.
When we adjourned in June, representatives of the Government told us that it would be possible for Bill C-55 to be studied in committee in the fall. That would have given an adequate opportunity for various groups who are concerned about the legislation, including expert witnesses and others, to appear before a committee of the House in order to give a thorough examination to the legislation. That was the case when the House adjourned at the end of June.
What has happened to change the Government's legislative agenda? Someone could point to the arrival of the boatload of people in Nova Scotia. Or they could point to two or three people who arrived in the Northwest Territories during the summer. If that is all it takes for the Government to change its political agenda, if that is all it takes for the Government to insist that we rush through legislation without adequate study, then obviously it is not concerned about the passage of good legislation.
To complicate matters more, we have a situation right now wherein we have a legislative committee of the House studying the so-called emergency legislation, Bill C-84. The committee is in session right now. At the present time it has expert witnesses in front of it. What the Government is trying to do by giving second reading to Bill C-55 this afternoon is to ensure that we have another committee studying Bill C-55 at the same time as we have a committee studying Bill C-84. What we will have is a situation in which two different committees of the House are studying legislation which is closely related and intertwined at the same time. This is a system which would guarantee that we end up with bad legislation. One committee will not know what the other is doing. We will be in a situation in which clauses that depend on each other will not be studied in the fashion in which they should be.
The Government is working by political impulse. The unfortunate thing is that it has a very bad reading of the political pulse of the nation. As a result, the Government is panicking. It is passing legislation which we can almost guarantee will be thrown out in the courts, just as has happened with legislation which the Government introduced before in a rush, in a so-called emergency.
It is evident from the tone of the debate that the Government and its back-benchers are trying to create fear and to build on fear across this land. You have heard, Mr. Speaker, cabinet Ministers, Prime Ministers and ordinary Members of Parliament talk about queue jumping. Your Honour has heard them talk about people arriving and abusing our system. Well, there are people abusing our system, but that is not what this legislation is about. This legislation is trying to hit those people who are helping honest refugees. This legislation will hit those people who do not have the proper documents because they come from countries where they cannot obtain those proper documents. For the Government, including the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), to talk about the fact that those refugees, or those so-called refugees, are queue jumpers is ignoring the fact that legitimate refugees and legitimate immigrants have a heck of a time getting into this country because of the bureaucratic mess that the Government has instituted and because the Government has not been able to overcome the past Liberal legislation.
As a result, the examples I raised yesterday and the example I will give now are not examples of refugees, or so-called refugees, abusing the system, therefore keeping out legitimate refugees and legitimate immigrants or people who want to join their families in Canada. The problem is that the Government has not addressed the real problems of family reunification. The Government has not dealt with the real problem of ensuring that legitimate immigrants come to the country.
The example which I wish to give today involves my having written to the Minister, the previous Minister and the Minister prior to that. The case to which I refer involves a Canadian whose family is from Peru. He cannot get his mother-in-law into the country. Why? Not because of refugees landing in Nova Scotia but because the woman cannot find her marriage certificate. 1 have written to the Minister asking for special consideration in this case, but my request has been denied. This is not a matter of a refugee landing in Nova Scotia and being denied access. It is an example of the Minister and the laws he is protecting and the bureaucratic system of which he is a part denying that woman access to Canada.
It is time that the Prime Minister, cabinet Ministers and Conservative MPs were honest with Canadians. We need real legislation to keep out the abusers. But we do not need the false rhetoric of the Conservatives. We need legislation that will keep out the abusers and that will punish the real smugglers.
We do not need legislation that punishes real refugees, those who cannot get papers, those humanitarians in Canada who
August 19, 1987

are concerned about trying to help refugees. That is what we have before us in this Bill. The fact that the Government wants to rush through consideration of this legislation, the fact that it wants to have two committees studying related legislation at the same time indicates a political agenda, a very corrupt agenda.
