speakeroldname: Mr. Blaine A. Thacker (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an honour to rise to speak to the amendments which have been proposed by the Senate and to encourage Members of the House of Commons to concur in them. There has been very close consultation and the nine amendments will make a very great difference to the Bill and our constructive policy development for the nation.
As you know, Mr. Speaker, the development of this Bill and Bill C-19, an Act respecting the Motor Vehicle Transport Act, has involved one of the most extensive consultation processes ever engaged in by a government in preparation of legislation. Release of Freedom to Move report in July, 1985, was followed by two sets of hearings by the House of Commons standing committee, one on Freedom to Move as a whole and one focused specifically on the North. Both of these involved hearings in various regions of the country.
I would once again like to thank the members of the standing committee from all Parties under the able leadership of the Hon. Member for Annapolis Valley-Hants (Mr. Nowlan) who spent virtually thousands of hours on this legislation. They would not have had to spend that time. It is possible to sit as a Member of Parliament and not do much, but these ladies and gentlemen did a lot of work for the public policy of this nation. I think they should be commended once again for the personal sacrifice that they made.
Following tabling and second reading of the Bills in the House of Commons, the Standing Committee on Transport held another set of hearings across the country. Hundreds of witnesses appeared and hundreds of briefs were received and reviewed. More recently the Senate Standing Committee on Transport and Communications has had the opportunity to review Bills C-18 and C-19 and has held hearings to receive firsthand, the views of 75 additional witnesses.
1 cannot stress too much that these Bills will help our producers and manufacturers. As a result of their improved competitive position they will be better able to maintain and create jobs in every region of the country.
The Government has undertaken to implement Bills C-18 and C-19 on January 1, 1988. Everyone affected is busy making plans to take advantage of the new opportunities as of that date.
Nine Senate amendments to Bill C-18 are now awaiting our approval. Seven of these are for the purpose of clarifying the wording of the French text, while another amendment corrects
a spelling error. The major amendment involves a stipulation that members of the new agency must be either Canadian citizens or permanent residents of Canada, which is surely a reasonable and indeed desirable qualification. There is no doubt that they would have been such in any event, but to have it enshrined in the statute is not a disagreeable proposition.
Allow me once again to elaborate on the benefits I anticipate once this Bill and its companion, Bill C-19, become law. These Bills will remove obstacles to innovation in both services offered and prices charged in the air, rail and trucking sectors. As a result, shippers will be more competitive and will be able to maintain existing jobs and create new ones in every region of the country.
A fundamental principle of these Bills is that transportation exists to serve the needs of shippers and travellers. Many of our producers, especially our resource producers, have faced severe difficulties in recent years and see these reforms as a necessary step in maintaining and improving their competitive position.
Bill C-18 provides workable remedies for captive rail shippers who have few practical recourses under the present law. It also provides many, for the first time, with competitive alternatives. For manufacturers, innovative service and freight packages in both the rail and trucking sectors will allow them to meet the demands of today's economy. Passage of the Bills will also give us better service and price packages from air carriers, which will benefit both leisure and business travellers.
Turning for a moment to safety, the first and overriding principle in the legislation is that the transportation system must be safe. Government's commitment to this principle will never waver. My colleagues will elaborate further tomorrow on just what that means. Section 3 of the new National Transportation Act enshrines this commitment in legislation for the first time.
I think Members should note that for the first time we actually have enshrined in legislation that safety is the highest priority. We have operated all these many years without that as the highest priority. It is now the highest priority, and I am sure all Members will find that to be a worthy principle.
I said at the outset that Bills C-18 and C-19 are based on extensive consultation. I would like to mention just a few examples of how the Government has listened and made changes. First, Bill C-18, as tabled in the House last November, recognized the principle that transportation is a key to regional economic development. Many witnesses and members of the Standing Committee on Transport felt that this should be strengthened. The Government listened and agreed.
Now the Bill states that the commercial viability of transportation links should be balanced with regional development objectives so that the economic strengths in each region can be realized. This principle will be part of the definition of public interest to be applied by the new agency in its decisions. We have operated all these many years without that as a
August 19, 1987

principle of the law. It is now a principle of the law. An efficient, effective and competitive transportation system is a prerequisite for lasting economic development in all regions. Bill C-18 will give us just such a system.
The Government of Canada is committed to ensuring that disabled persons have access to the transportation system. This commitment is reflected in the policy statement in Section 3 of the Bill. While it was the original intent of the Government to fulfil its pledge through human rights legislation, we were convinced otherwise by the sincere representations made before the House standing committee. Accordingly, the Bill was amended to give the new agency the power to enforce accessibility standards for the disabled. Again, for the first time in our entire legislative history disabled people are recognized statutorily for the purpose of transportation.
In all, there were approximately 50 amendments made to Bill C-18 by the House of Commons, and now an additional nine by the Senate. Throughout the development of these Bills, the need to have a balanced package, especially with respect to the interests of shippers and carriers, has been held firmly in mind. The need to make Canadian products more competitive in domestic and international markets where the costs of transportation are a vital element has also been a primary consideration.
I believe that Bill C-18 is a balanced package. It is not simply deregulation; it removes unnecessary regulations and it protects the public interest where that is really necessary, for example, in the special regime for northern air services. Thus, Bill C-18 is truly a made-in-Canada policy.
I therefore encourage my hon. colleagues to support the Senate amendments to Bill C-18. It is clear that we need these amendments. The benefits are also clear. Now is the time to finish the job of making these reforms a reality.

Mr. Speaker, I thank my colleagues across the way for agreeing to permit me to speak this evening to the matter now before the House. As you may know, Mr. Speaker, the whole question of transport deregulation, particularly as it affects deregulation in the rail sector, has been a matter of pressing concern to me coming as I do from a riding in which life is so bound up in the transportation sector. 1 have the CNR main back shops, Transcona shops in my riding and Symington yard very near.
In Winnipeg in general the question of the future of rail transportation and the future of Winnipeg within the broader framework of rail transportation is a matter of ongoing concern and debate, as Hon. Members will know from the many occasions on which I have asked the Government questions in the House about the various aspects of Winnipeg's future as it pertains to transportation deregulation.
I wonder, Mr. Speaker, if I could appeal to the Hon. Members. I am having a hard time hearing myself over the conversation.
National Transportation Act, 1987
First, we are debating amendments which have come back to us from the Senate. It is my understanding that those amendments are not particularly offensive but, rather, ones that were agreed upon in the Senate between government and opposition Members. For instance, they include an amendment to require Canadian citizenship of members on the National Transportation Agency. There are various amendments which bring the French and English text into line. They are not a matter of controversy.
However, we should not let that obscure the fact that the whole deregulation package itself is deeply controversial. There is, particularly between the Progressive Conservative Government and the New Democratic Party, a very serious division of opinion about how our transportation system ought to be ordered in this country.
1 notice that, unlike the situation with respect to Bill C-22, despite the great deal of Liberal rhetoric in the House of Commons about the current Government's plans for deregulation, the Liberals in the Senate did not move any significant amendments to the transportation deregulation. After all was said and done, there was no real battle waged in the Senate over deregulation. The Liberals and Conservatives were basically able to agree on deregulation.
I believe that Canadians who are against the current deregulation package should take keen note of the fact that deregulation had its roots in Liberal government policy preceding the election of 1984. There is a great deal of overlap and consensus between the Liberal and Conservative Parties with respect to deregulation.
The only real opponent in the House of Commons to what the Government is trying to do to our transportation sector is the New Democratic Party. Today is a very timely day to be considering the matter of deregulation in one of the final stages before Bill C-18 and Bill C-19 become law.
At this very time we are seeing one of the fruits of the anticipation of deregulation in the whole matter of negotiations going on between the railway unions and Canadian National and Canadian Pacific Railways.
It was once said of deregulation in the United States that deregulation turned out to be the biggest piece of anti-labour legislation that was ever passed in that country. In as far as the initial arguments of the railways for a 5 per cent wage rollback and a reduced initial wage were based on the anticipation of deregulation, the very same thing is beginning to happen here in Canada. Deregulation will become the grounds on which a great many working Canadians who are now well paid will become less well paid as the years roll by and the effects of deregulation and the irrational competition it brings into being in Canada come to be experienced.
I want to offer the empirical proof of the very arguments that the railways are now using with respect to the competition they expect to receive from American railways as a result of

National Transportation Act, 1987
the provision in Bill C-18 for competitive line rates. This would allow American railways to compete for Canadian traffic directly.
I was interested to hear the Hon. Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport (Mr. Thacker) say that transportation was to be the key to regional economic development and that this was one of the mainstays of the Government's belief with respect to deregulation. The Hon. Parliamentary Secretary comes from western Canada. Canadian railways will be put into a position whereby goods that they normally carry may well be carried to the border points south of Alberta in Montana, and transported across the northern United States either to destinations in the northeastern United States or in eastern Canada. How does that serve the regional economic development of western Canada, when all the jobs in between, both railway associated jobs and the spin-off economic potential, will be put at risk by that particular measure?
This issue becomes a matter of national integrity for me. This legislation would let American railways compete in this manner with our two railways. It will put our two railways, CN and CP, at each other's throats by competing with each other and for the traffic now carried by trucks. As a result, there will be more pressure on the railways to abandon trackage. That will mean more pressure on provincial Governments as that trackage is abandoned and more trucks are used on the roads.
Furthermore, that transportation will not necessarily be by Canadian trucks. It may well be that Canadian trucking firms will be put in severe jeopardy as a result of the entry of American trucking firms into the Canadian market. There are many people involved in trucking in Winnipeg who are concerned about that possibility.
Let us consider the cumulative impact on the region of western Canada, because the Minister cited regional economic development as one of the elements of the Government's objectives when it decided to deregulate. There will be more rail line abandonment and heavier use of roads, the cost of which will be picked up by provincial Governments that are already experiencing a great deal of fiscal pressure from the Government in terms of costs that were not previously passed on and various cut-backs that have taken place.
The community infrastructure of many smaller communities in western Canada will be put at risk as the elevators and other operations shut down. As people move out of these communities, there will be pressure on the remaining citizens to fund the schools and other community services. These effects will not take place overnight, but during a longer period.
The Conservative Government says that it is the values and lifestyle of small communities that are the backbone of this country, where we find the very best of what it means to be Canadian. The Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills has heard me argue many times that I Find it ironic that a Conservative Government says it cannot fight that battle and must get on board and follow that trend by deregulating and
taking other steps so the process will come to a conclusion as quickly as possible. I would think that it would want to resist that trend and try to find ways of structuring our economy so that these types of communities could continue to exist in a healthy and lively atmosphere.
We believe that is possible, but it means having a critical rather than an accommodating attitude toward the trends in the market-place. That is what clearly defines the difference between the Conservatives and the New Democrats. Our approach is to think critically about what is happening in the market-place, globally, nationally, and locally, and to address how we can resist those trends in the market-place that negatively affect the quality of human life and so structure our economic life that those negative impacts will not occur. Having said that, I believe the difference between us and the Conservatives is that they know these trends are taking place. They say: "That is the invisible hand of Adam Smith. That is the market-place working itself out in the universe". They say there is nothing they can do about it, that all they can do is try to accommodate those trends in such a way as to make maximum economic advantage of it for those people who are already well placed in the market-place. That is the great divide between the Conservative Party and the New Democratic Party. The relative complacency with which the Liberal Party has regarded this whole debate on deregulation shows that, really, when it comes to these kinds of issues-and 1 admit there are perhaps a couple of issues about which there are fundamental differences between the Liberals and the Conservatives-there is really no difference between the Liberal Party and the Conservative party.
I go back to a matter raised in the House earlier today when the Hon. Member for Winnipeg-Fort Garry (Mr. Axworthy) rose and had the nerve to chastise the Government for not living up to its commitments to western Canada vis-a-vis rail line upgrading. He cited the lay-off in Winnipeg at the Butt Weld in Transcona, a place where I used to work, as evidence of the lack of willingness of the CNR to live up to its promises. It was both the Liberals and the Conservatives who not so long ago in this place argued for a change in the Crow rate on the basis that if it were to be changed there would be a new era for rail transportation in western Canada. They said this would mean massive investment in double tracking, tunnels and in a great many other ways. The people in the shops in Winnipeg were led to believe that if we just changed the Crow rate there would be the dawning of a new era with respect to rail transportation. The very opposite has happened in many respects.
Since the change in the Crow rate, we have seen still more reductions in the number of employees at both major railways. We have seen the shut-down of major shops. I am thinking of Moncton in particular with respect to CN. We have seen rationalization, so called, going on in both railways, which has

not had the beneficial effect which was promised during the Crow-rate debate.
So what we have before us is the beginning of the end of an entire way of life in Canada and, in particular, in western Canada. 1 admit, as someone younger than the Hon. Member for Lethbridge-Foothills, that I took it all for granted. I thought this was the way Canada was and that there would be no debate on that. I never really took seriously-although I now wish I had-the possibility that we could some day elect a government that would so directly attack the very economic infrastructure of Canada, and particularly western Canada, through transportation deregulation. Yet that is what is happening.
We will come to see that that is what Bill C-18 represents. To be fair, I tend to concentrate too much on matters having to do with rail transportation. I think it would be in order for a moment to speak about airline deregulation. Some questions have been asked in the House in recent days. I certainly do not intend to hang anything I have to say on any particular accident or anything like that, but the fact is that there is growing concern about the effects on safety of deregulation in the United States. The Parliamentary Secretary, when asked about this is quick to point out that Canada is in a very different situation. We have a lot fewer flights, we have less density of population and so on, and we are really not to be compared. It is a point well taken to a degree. However, the fact is that we are learning from the American experience that deregulation does put unhealthy pressures on airlines to cut corners, to push equipment a little harder and a little longer than it should be, and to have fewer employees than they should have because they are competing with someone else. An airline decides to cut staff in order to be competitive and keep its prices down. We know this happens. It really has nothing to do with whether or not the Government is genuinely committed to safety as its highest priority. It is nice that it is in the legislation. No one argues with that. The Parliamentary Secretary pointed that out. But having a preamble or whatever in the legislation is not enough. It has to be backed up with a
National Transportation Act, 1987
system that actually lends itself to safety, or a government that is committed, having created a situation which does not lend itself to safety, to having the necessary staff around to do the kinds of inspection, enforcement and investigative work that will actually create the kind of commitment to safety about which the Parliamentary Secretary speaks. We do not believe that is being done.
No one is saying the Government is out to create an unsafe system. We just think its faith-and it is really taking a leap of faith in this respect-is unjustified.
I just want to reiterate the complete and total opposition of the New Democratic Party to the deregulation legislation which has previously been before this House and which is now before the House in the form of amendments sent back to this House from the Senate. In my eight years and some months in this House, I cannot think of anything that will have a more negative impact on the economic and social well-being in the long run of the people in my constituency.
